mediaItem.network: Lava for Good podcasts, Signal Company No. 1
mediaItem.seriesType: Episodic Series (each episode is generally a standalone story)
mediaItem.keyStats: Evaristo Salas was incarcerated for 27 years and 3 months for a crime he did not commit. His conviction was overturned due to prosecutorial misconduct and fabricated evidence.
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction with Maggie Freeling tells the harrowing story of Evaristo Salas, wrongfully convicted of murder at the age of 16 and imprisoned for over 27 years.  Growing up in a chaotic environment and joining a gang for protection, Evaristo became a target of local police.  Despite maintaining his innocence, fabricated informant testimony and a questionable eyewitness identification, influenced by hypnosis, led to his conviction.  After decades of struggle and persistent efforts, new evidence of police misconduct and recanted testimony surfaced, leading to his exoneration in 2023.  The episode highlights systemic issues of racial bias, police misconduct, and the devastating impact of wrongful convictions on individuals and families.  Since his release, Evaristo is dedicated to giving back to his community and advocating for justice reform.

featuredIndividual.crimeConvictedOf: First-degree murder and unlawful possession of a weapon
contributingFactorsRaw: False informant testimony (fabricated by Bill Brun under police pressure and payment)
Eyewitness misidentification (Ophelia Gonzalez, potentially influenced by hypnosis)
Police misconduct (Detective Revard paying informant, witness intimidation, racial bias, withholding evidence)
Ineffective trial defense (potentially, though not explicitly stated as a major factor)
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Washington Innocence Project (assisted with post-conviction legal efforts)
Lava for Good podcasts (brought attention to the case through the podcast)
Documentary team (investigation by Joe Burlinger's team for a documentary)
innocenceLawyersRaw: Laura Shaver, post-conviction attorney, started her own firm and took Evaristo's case pro bono. She meticulously investigated the case, uncovered evidence of police misconduct and undisclosed evidence, and successfully argued for a new trial, ultimately leading to exoneration.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Likely appears in exoneree databases, needs to be confirmed.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: Jose Ariola was shot and killed in his apartment parking lot in Sunnyside, Washington, in November 1995. His girlfriend, Ophelia Gonzalez, witnessed two figures near the truck before the shooting.
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Eyewitness testimony from Ophelia Gonzalez identifying Evaristo in a photo lineup.
Informant testimony from Bill Brun claiming Evaristo confessed at a park.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: George Trejo, the defense attorney, argued misidentification and presented an alibi witness, Sylvia from a convenience store, who placed Evaristo near his home around the time of the shooting. However, this defense was unsuccessful.  He also made a record of witness intimidation by Officer Revard.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Recantation of testimony by informant Bill Brun, admitting Revard paid him and provided drugs to falsely implicate Evaristo.
Discovery of receipts showing payments to Bill Brun by the Sunnyside Police Department, contradicting initial denials.
Information suggesting Ophelia Gonzalez's identification may have been influenced by hypnosis, which was not disclosed at trial.
Evidence of a lawsuit against Officer Revard for racial discrimination, suggesting a pattern of biased policing.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Not detailed in the transcript. The focus is on Evaristo's wrongful conviction, not the identification of the actual perpetrator.

keyQuotesRaw: Evaristo: "I was incarcerated for 27 years, three months, for murder and a commit."
Debbie (sister): "I was always protecting him regardless. It was no matter where we were at, at a very young age, so right now I still protect them."
Evaristo describing police harassment: "If we're walking somewhere, they'd pull us over. If I was walking somewhere by myself, they'd pull me over, search me, pat me down, call me names, yell at me."

Evaristo on being convicted: "It was a feeling like, of course, you know, of course. Because at that point in my life, I have taken so many punches and dealt with so many, you know, horrific moments of my life. And it was just like, okay, of course, you know, that's exactly what's going to happen."
Evaristo after exoneration: "I survived." and his father's response: "Me, oh, I'm still alive."
systemicIssuesRaw: Police misconduct: Fabricating evidence, witness intimidation, racial bias, failure to disclose exculpatory evidence.
Ineffective assistance of counsel (potential, though not explicitly detailed).
The use of unreliable informant testimony.
Potential issues with eyewitness identification and the use of hypnosis in investigations.
Racial profiling and targeting of Hispanic youth by law enforcement.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Implicit call to action to support Innocence Projects and organizations fighting wrongful convictions. The episode implicitly calls for police accountability and reform, and for a re-evaluation of the use of informant testimony and eyewitness identification in criminal cases.
personalNarrativeRaw: Evaristo's personal narrative highlights resilience and determination in the face of injustice. Despite enduring horrific prison conditions and losing decades of his life, he maintained hope and focused on proving his innocence.  His final thoughts emphasize survival and giving back to his community, demonstrating a commitment to positive change and helping others avoid similar tragedies.
